title: Before I shaped you
sum: Jeremiah, a priest's son from Anathoth, tells how the LORD called him. The book is dated to the reigns of Josiah, Jehoiakim and Zedekiah, from 627 to the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC (1:1-3). The LORD says he knew Jeremiah and set him apart before he was born, and appointed him a prophet to the nations (1:5). Jeremiah answers that he is only a boy. The LORD touches his mouth and puts his words there, and gives him a work of six verbs: to pull up and pull down, to destroy and demolish, to build and to plant (1:6-10).

Two visions follow, each introduced by a question, 'What do you see?'. An almond branch tells Jeremiah that the LORD is watching over his word to carry it out (1:11-12). A pot on a fanned fire, tilted away from the north, tells him that disaster will pour out from the north on the whole land, as northern kings set their thrones at Jerusalem's gates to pass judgment (1:13-16). The chapter ends with the LORD's charge: stand up and speak, and he will make Jeremiah a fortress against kings, officials, priests and people. They will fight him, but they will not beat him (1:17-19).
readings: Read as a call story

The chapter follows the pattern of the calls of Moses, Gideon and Isaiah: a commission, an objection, a promise of God's presence and a sign. Its purpose is to say that Jeremiah's unwelcome words are not his own.
Read as the book's opening charter

Others stress that chapter 1 states the whole book in small: the six verbs (1:10) look ahead to judgment and rebuilding, the almond and the pot to the word and the foe, and the fortress (1:18) to the struggles of the prophet. The chapter may have been shaped late, once the book was complete.

views.H: The call is dated to 627 BC, the thirteenth year of Josiah. Five years later came the finding of the law scroll and Josiah's reform (622, 2 Kings 22-23), of which Jeremiah says nothing. Jeremiah's work then covers the death of Josiah (609), Carchemish (605), the deportation of 597 and the fall of 586. The foe from the north was identified in different ways (see the note at 1:14).
views.C: Many scholars think 1:1-3 was written by an editor, since it speaks of Jeremiah in the third person and sums up a ministry that was over, and that the call report itself was shaped by Deuteronomy's language (1:7, 9, compare Deuteronomy 18:18). The Greek omits several phrases (see the variants at 1:17 and 1:18), supporting the view that the Hebrew text grew after the Greek's source was copied (Tov; Bogaert). The Greek of chapters 2-3 differs in many more places than the first chapter (see the variants at 2:2, 2:16, 2:34, 3:1-3 and 3:19).
views.J: The first chapters are read in the synagogue on the first of the three Sabbaths of rebuke before the Ninth of Av (1:1-2:3, Ashkenazi custom). Rashi dates God's knowledge of Jeremiah to Adam, and compares Jeremiah to Moses, the prophet 'like' whom the LORD would raise others (Deuteronomy 18:18): both prophesied for forty years.
views.X: Paul describes his own call in the words of Jeremiah 1:5 and Isaiah 49:1 (Galatians 1:15-16). Many Christian writers have seen in Jeremiah the pattern of a prophet who suffers for the word, and a figure of Christ. Churches differ on what 1:5 teaches about the unborn (see the card below).
views.F: Chapter 1 is a call, and little in it is waiting for a future fulfillment: the six verbs were carried out in Jeremiah's own day. Some readers who look for an end-time fulfillment point to the 'nations' of 1:5 and 1:10 and take the oracles against them (46-51) as a pattern for God's dealing with the nations at the end.

deep.b:
The Hebrew text is the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), read through the site's Hebrew text, with the machine list of its Ketiv/Qere readings. In chapters 1-6 that list has several that matter (2:20, 2:25, 2:27, 3:2, 4:19, 6:7, 6:29) and many that are spelling.

The Dead Sea Scrolls were read through the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription (the ETCBC edition). In chapters 1-6 they are thin: only 4QJer-c (4Q72) preserves any words, parts of 4:5 and 4:13-16, and it agrees with the Hebrew text we have, apart from a waw. No scroll of Jeremiah preserves any other verse of these six chapters, so for them the only witnesses to an earlier form of the text are the Greek and the later versions. A note says 'no scroll preserves' where it matters.

In this part 'the Greek' means Swete's edition (Codex Vaticanus), read directly; Ziegler's critical text was not read, and the variants are named by Swete's codex. The Latin Vulgate is cited only where a variant names the source (Bible Gateway's printing for 3:1); the Targum and the Peshitta are not cited. Rashi's commentary was read on Sefaria for 1:5, 3:1, 3:16, 4:10 and 6:16.

The Greek is a little shorter. It has 'the word of God' for 'the words of Jeremiah' in 1:1 and usually leaves out 'the LORD declares' and similar short phrases. It reads 'a rod of a nut tree' in 1:11, 'a cauldron' in 1:13 and 'it will be kindled' in 1:14. Longer differences are given as variants: 1:17 (a promise in place of a threat) and 1:18 (no iron pillar, no priests). Where the Hebrew has 'the clans of the northern kingdoms' (1:15) the Greek has 'all the kingdoms from the north of the earth'.

Jeremiah's commission looks both ways. Four verbs are about destruction (pull up, pull down, destroy, demolish) and two about building (build, plant). The order matters: the judgment comes first, as the first half of the book shows, and the rebuilding is the content of the 'Book of Consolation' (30-33). The book itself returns to the verbs when it talks about its message to a nation (18:7-10) and when it explains the fall of Jerusalem (31:28; 42:10; 45:4).

echoes: Deuteronomy 18:18; Exodus 3:11-12; Exodus 4:10-12; Isaiah 6:6-7; Isaiah 49:1; Ezekiel 2:8-3:3; Galatians 1:15-16; Amos 8:1-2; Jeremiah 15:19-21

traditions.q: How do churches use Jeremiah 1:5 in teaching on the unborn?
views: Human life is to be respected and protected absolutely from the moment of conception; the Catechism quotes 'Before I formed you in the womb I knew you' among the biblical signs of this (Catechism of the Catholic Church 2270).

The Church has condemned abortion since its earliest days: the Didache says 'you shall not murder a child by abortion' (2:2), and Basil of Caesarea's canons treat the destruction of the unborn as murder and decline to distinguish formed from unformed (Letter 188, canon 2). Orthodox teaching does not rest on Jeremiah 1:5 alone.

Lutheran bodies differ. The Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod's Commission on Theology and Church Relations, in a study prepared after a 2023 convention request (Abortion: Past Truths, Current Challenges), cites Psalm 139:13-16, Jeremiah 1:5 and Isaiah 49:1 for the worth of life in the womb. The Evangelical Lutheran Church in America's 1991 social statement says that a developing life in the womb has no absolute right to be born, and a pregnant woman no absolute right to end a pregnancy, and it opposes both having no regulation of abortion and laws that ban it in all circumstances.

The Westminster Larger Catechism, held by Presbyterian churches, reads the sixth commandment as forbidding the taking of one's own life or another's except in public justice, lawful war or necessary defense (questions 135-136). The Presbyterian Church in America's 1978 committee report on abortion, one Reformed application, cites Jeremiah 1:5 and Psalm 139:13-16 to show God's care for a child before birth, and holds that abortion breaks the sixth commandment. The Reformed family has no single statement.

The Church of England's Mission and Public Affairs Council has described its position as strong opposition to abortion alongside strictly limited conditions in which abortion may be morally preferable to any available alternative (2005), and has called the foetus 'a human life with the potential to develop relationships, think, pray, choose and love' (2011). The statements read do not rest the case on Jeremiah 1:5.

The Southern Baptist Convention's Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article XV) calls Christians to 'speak on behalf of the unborn' and to defend the sanctity of human life 'from conception to natural death'. Baptists have no single creed, and some Baptist bodies take other positions.

The United Methodist Social Principles speak of the 'sanctity of unborn human life' and are 'reluctant to approve abortion', but also recognize 'tragic conflicts of life with life that may justify abortion'. They do not use Jeremiah 1:5 to settle when personhood begins.

settings.by: The LORD, in words and two visions, to Jeremiah
settings.to: Jeremiah, a young man ('a boy') from a priestly family at Anathoth, in his own village or on a road near it
settings.when: In the thirteenth year of Josiah, 627 BC (1:2)
settings.why: To make Jeremiah the LORD's spokesman before he spoke a word: the words are the LORD's, the opposition was foreseen, and his protection is promised. The two visions give him the message in advance, a word that will be carried out and a foe from the north.
settings.readers: For the exiles who read the finished book, the call was proof that the man who announced the fall of Jerusalem was sent by the LORD, and that his hard words were fulfilled.
views: The book gives 627 BC. William Holladay holds that the thirteenth year dates Jeremiah's birth, and puts his call later, in Jehoiakim's reign. Most take the heading at face value.

title: Broken cisterns
sum: The LORD sends Jeremiah to call out in Jerusalem's ears. He remembers a bride who followed him through the wilderness, Israel the holy firstfruits (2:1-3). Then he puts his case against the house of Jacob: what wrong did their ancestors find in him that they went after emptiness and became empty? They never asked, 'Where is the LORD?', not the priests, nor the rulers, nor the prophets (2:4-8). No nation has ever traded its gods, yet his people have traded their Glory for what cannot help them (2:9-12).

The case turns to the people's own acts: two wrongs, leaving the spring of living water and digging cracked cisterns (2:13); Israel plundered like a slave though born in the house (2:14-19); the choice vine gone bad, the stain that no soap can take out (2:20-22); and the wild she-camel and the wild donkey of the next lines, who cannot stop running after the Baals (2:23-25). The people claim they are innocent and the LORD takes them to court (2:29-35). The last word is a warning not to put hope in Egypt, as they were shamed by Assyria (2:36-37).
readings: Read as a covenant lawsuit

The chapter is a courtroom scene (a rib, 'case'). The LORD is both plaintiff and judge; he questions the accused (2:5, 14, 17, 29), calls the nations as witnesses (2:10-12) and states the charge. The verdict is delivered in the later chapters.
Read as a marriage poem

Others stress the picture of marriage that runs through 2:2-3:5: the bride in the wilderness, the broken yoke and the prostitute, the wild animals in heat, the ornaments the bride forgets. It is Hosea's picture, and the theme of love betrayed fits the chapter's tone better than a legal argument.

views.H: Many historians place these poems early in Jeremiah's ministry, before Josiah's reform in 622, because the picture of open idolatry (2:20, 27-28) fits those years; the mention of Egypt and Assyria (2:18, 36) suits the time before 609, when Assyria still counted. Others tie 2:16 to Neco's killing of Josiah at Megiddo in 609 and date the chapter to Jehoiakim's early years.
views.C: The chapter is poetry from the oldest layer of the book, in the view of Duhm and Mowinckel (their source A); its opening (2:1-3) is often held to be a self-contained piece. The Greek lacks 2:1, 2:2a and the clause about leading on the road in 2:17 (see the variants), which may show editorial additions in the longer edition.
views.J: 2:4-28 with 3:4 is the haftarah of the second Sabbath of rebuke before the Ninth of Av, in the Ashkenazi custom.
views.X: Jesus' offer of 'living water' (John 4:10-14; 7:37-38) takes up the image of 2:13. Paul uses 2:11 with Psalm 106:20 in Romans 1:23 for the exchange of the glory of God for images.
views.F: The chapter is largely about the past. Some readers take the remembering of Israel's bridal days as a promise of a renewed betrothal at the end (Hosea 2:14-20), and the firstfruits of 2:3 as a sign of Israel's future place among the nations.

deep.b: The Greek lacks 2:1 and the first sentence of 2:2, and the clause 'while he was leading you on the road' in 2:17. In 2:2 it has Israel follow 'the Holy One of Israel' and has no unsown wilderness land. In 2:16 it has 'the sons of Memphis and Tahpanhes knew you and mocked you', and in 2:34 'not in tunnels did I find them, but under every oak'. It gives 'Memphis' for 'Noph' (2:16), 'says the Lord your God' for 'the Lord GOD of Armies declares' (2:19), and the transliterated 'Carmel' for 'a land of orchards' (2:7). In 2:28 it adds a second line about the streets of Jerusalem (see the variant). In 2:20 it agrees with the Ketiv, 'I will not serve', and in 2:25 and 2:27 it sides with the Qere and the Ketiv respectively (see the variants).

The question of 2:6 and 2:8 is both a sign of the people's forgetting and the opposite of a prayer. It is the opposite of the nations' taunt in Psalm 79:10 and Joel 2:17, 'Where is their God?'; in Jeremiah's day it is what the people should have asked and did not. The same charge falls on the priests, the rulers, and the prophets (2:8), the three groups the book will name again and again.

echoes: Hosea 2:14-15; Hosea 9:10; Ezekiel 16:8; Isaiah 5:1-7; Psalm 106:20; Romans 1:23; John 4:10-14; 2 Kings 17:15; Deuteronomy 32:10-18

settings.what: The LORD's case against his people
settings.to: Jerusalem and 'the house of Jacob, and all the clans of the house of Israel' (2:2, 4), in public
settings.when: Not dated. Many place it in Josiah's early years, before the reform of 622; some in Jehoiakim's early years, after Neco defeated Josiah in 609 (2:16-18).
settings.why: To make the people see what they have done as a breach of love, not just of law: the LORD brought them out and led them, and they exchanged him for gods that cannot save. The case aims to break through their claim that they are innocent (2:23, 35) so that the call to turn back in 3:1-4:4 can be heard.
settings.readers: The exiles read it as an explanation of why the city and Temple fell, and as the LORD's own answer to the question 'Where is the LORD?'
views: John Bright places the poems before the reform of 622, when the old cults were still open.
Others tie 2:16 to Neco's defeat of Josiah and date the chapter to the early years of Jehoiakim.

title: Turn back, you who turned away
sum: The chapter opens with a law. If a man divorces his wife and she marries another, he cannot take her back, since she is 'polluted' (Deuteronomy 24:1-4). Judah has had many lovers, yet the LORD says, 'Return to me' (3:1). The bare hills, the withheld rain and the forehead of a prostitute are the evidence (3:2-5). Then the LORD tells Jeremiah, in the days of Josiah, of two sisters. Israel, the northern kingdom, played the prostitute and was divorced and sent into exile; her sister Judah saw it, was not afraid, and did the same (3:6-10). Israel, who turned away, has shown herself more in the right than treacherous Judah (3:11).

The message to the north is an invitation: 'Turn back, you who turned away'. The LORD is loyal and will not hold a grudge forever; they need only admit their guilt (3:12-14). The promises that follow are the first of Jeremiah's pictures of restoration: shepherds after the LORD's heart, a Jerusalem so full of the LORD's presence that no one will miss the ark, nations gathering to it, and Judah and Israel walking together out of the north (3:15-18). The LORD hoped that they would call him 'Father', and they betrayed him (3:19-20). The chapter ends with the sound of weeping and a confession put into the people's mouths (3:21-25).
readings: Read as one speech
Chapters 2:1-4:4 may be one sermon that moves from the charge (2) through the invitation (3) to the call to act (4:1-4). The word 'turn' is its thread.
Read as separate pieces

Others find at least three pieces: 3:1-5 (poetry), 3:6-11 (a prose report, dated to Josiah, in the language of Deuteronomy) and 3:12-25 (poetry and prose together), brought together because they share the words 'turn' and 'prostitute'.

views.H: 3:6-11 is dated to Josiah's reign and may belong to the time when Josiah's reform reached the old northern kingdom (2 Kings 23:15-20). If so, 3:12, 'toward the north', was an invitation to the remnant of Israel. The verdict on Judah's turning 'with a lie' (3:10) shows that the reform did not go deep.
views.C: Many scholars treat 3:6-13 as prose added to the older poem and 3:15-18 as a later addition from the exile, since they look ahead to the end of Israel's and Judah's division and to the nations' coming to Jerusalem (compare Isaiah 2:2-4). The Greek lacks 'to the name of the LORD, to Jerusalem' in 3:17 and differs in 3:1-3, 3:7 and 3:19 (see the variants).
views.J: Rashi reads 3:1 as the LORD's longing to take Israel back, and 3:16 as promising a time when the whole assembly will be so holy that the ark will not be needed. The Talmud reports that Josiah hid the ark (Yoma 52b).
views.X: Many Christian readers see in 3:1 a picture of grace beyond law: God does what a husband may not do. 3:15 is often applied to the pastors of the church, and 3:16-17 to the church as the new Jerusalem (Galatians 4:26; Hebrews 12:22).
views.F: 3:17-18 (the nations gathering to Jerusalem, Judah and Israel together coming from the north) is taken by many premillennial and dispensational readers as a prediction of the millennial kingdom; Jewish readers connect it to the days of the Messiah. Others see it fulfilled in the return from Babylon, or in the church.

deep.h: Turn: the word that runs through the chapter
deep.b: The Hebrew root shuv and its relatives appear about a dozen times in 3:1-4:2. It means to turn around, to return, and so to turn away or turn back. The Plain English Translation translates it 'turn' throughout so the reader can follow the play: 'turn back' (3:12, 14, 22), 'Israel, who turned away' (meshuvah), 'children who turn away' (shovavim) and 'your turning away' (3:22). The pun is the point: the same road can lead away from the LORD or back to him. For the history of the root see William Holladay's study.

deep.h: Deuteronomy 24 and the question of return
deep.b: Jeremiah quotes the law of Deuteronomy 24:1-4, which forbids a man to take back a wife who has married another. The law protects the second marriage and guards against treating marriage as a revolving door. Jeremiah uses it to show the force of what the LORD is doing. Interpreters take it three ways: (1) the LORD is showing grace that goes beyond the law; (2) the question is rhetorical and the answer is no, and the LORD's call to turn back is a new act of mercy that does not rest on the law; (3) in the Greek, the wife is the one who returns (see the variant), which turns it into a question about Israel's return as a wife. In all of them the surprise is that the LORD still says 'return'.

Besides the variants, the Greek has 'I am merciful' (eleemon) where the Hebrew says 'I am loyal' (3:12) and 'I will rule over you' (katakyrieuso) for 'I am your husband' (3:14). In 3:19 it has 'So be it, Lord' where the Hebrew begins 'How I will set you ...' (see the variant). In 3:24 it has 'shame' (aischune) where the Hebrew has bosheth; the idea is the same, but the Greek does not make the name of Baal visible. The differences in 3:1 change the sense, and so they are given in full.

echoes: Deuteronomy 24:1-4; Hosea 2:2-23; Isaiah 50:1; Ezekiel 23; Hosea 14:1-3; Jeremiah 31:21-22; 1 Samuel 13:14; 2 Maccabees 2:4-8; Isaiah 2:2-4; Zechariah 8:20-23

settings.what: The two sisters and the call to turn back
settings.by: The LORD to Jeremiah, to be called out toward the north (3:12)
settings.to: Israel, the old northern kingdom, now in exile and in the ruins of Samaria, and Judah, who must overhear it
settings.when: 'In the days of King Josiah' (3:6); some place it in the middle of his reign, around the time of his reform
settings.why: To warn Judah by the example of her sister and, at the same time, to open a door for the exiles of the north: a divorced wife can come back. The call needs only an honest admission of guilt (3:13).
settings.readers: The exiles of both kingdoms, reading it as the LORD's promise that division and exile would not be the last word.
views: Commentators who accept the heading, such as Bright, take it as a message from Jeremiah's early years, aimed at the north during Josiah's reform.
Others, following Nicholson and Thiel on the prose of the book, see the report of 3:6-13 as the work of editors who set the sisters story inside Josiah's reign to comment on it.

settings.what: The promise of shepherds, the lost ark and the gathered nations
settings.by: The LORD, within the call to the north
settings.to: Israel, first the exiles of the north addressed in 3:12, and through them Judah (3:18)
settings.when: Not separately dated. It stands inside the Josiah-era call of 3:6-4:2; some scholars treat 3:15-18 as an addition from the exile.
settings.why: To say that the turning back asked for in 3:12-14 leads somewhere: rulers after the LORD's own heart, a Jerusalem so full of his presence that the ark is not missed, the nations gathering to it, and the two kingdoms joined again.
settings.readers: The exiles, for whom the ark was gone and the two kingdoms long divided; the promise said that the loss would not be final.
views: Taken with the heading, the promise is an early word to the remnant of the north, 'toward the north' (3:12).
Others read 3:15-18 as an addition from the exile, since it looks ahead to a Jerusalem without the ark and a reunited people (the critical view above).

settings.by: The LORD gives the words; the speakers are 'the Israelites', repentant
settings.to: The people, as the words they ought to say
settings.when: Not dated; a model confession before the return
settings.why: To show repentance in words, so the people can use them. It starts with the LORD's invitation, 'Turn back', and ends with the admission that the ancestors and the present generation have both sinned.
settings.readers: The exiles, who could use it as their prayer of repentance (compare Daniel 9).

title: The ram's horn in the land
sum: The message closes the call of chapter 3 with a choice. If Israel turns back, the nations will bless themselves by the LORD, but the turning must reach the heart: 'Be circumcised for the LORD, and take away the foreskins of your hearts' (4:1-4). Then comes the alarm. A ram's horn is blown in Judah, people are told to run for the walled cities, and a lion from the north has set out to make the land a waste (4:5-9). Jeremiah accuses the LORD of having deceived the people with promises of peace while the sword is at the throat (4:10).

The invasion is described in sudden pictures: clouds, chariots and a call to wash the heart clean (4:11-18). Then a cry of pain, 'My innards, my innards!' (4:19-22). The vision of 4:23-26 is the center of the chapter: the speaker looks four times, and sees the earth shapeless and empty, the lights gone, the mountains shaking, no human being, the birds fled and the orchard land a wilderness. The LORD says the land will be a desolation, but he will not make a complete end (4:27-28). The chapter ends with the city dressed up for lovers who turn on her, and Daughter Zion gasping like a woman in first labor (4:29-31).
readings: Read as a vision of the army
4:23-26 can be taken as the poet's view of what the invasion will do: the land emptied of people, fields and towns so that it seems the world was undone.
Read as a vision of creation reversed

Others stress the language of Genesis 1: the poem takes creation apart in reverse, until nothing is left but the shapeless earth (Fishbane). The army is real, but the poem shows what is at stake, the order of the world itself.

views.H: The ram's horn and the refugees (4:5-6) fit a time when an invader was close. For the conquest of Judah the dates suggest 605-597 and 588-586, when Babylon came; for 627-620, a Scythian or other northern raid has been proposed (Herodotus 1.105). Whatever the army, the poems show Jeremiah's knowledge that the danger was real.
views.C: Many critics treat the poetry of 4:5-31 as the work of Jeremiah himself (Duhm and Mowinckel's source A). 4QJer-c preserves parts of 4:5 and 4:13-16 and agrees with the Hebrew text. The Greek differs in 4:1-2, 4:11 and 4:19 (see the variants).
views.J: The call in 4:4 to circumcise the heart repeats Moses' words in Deuteronomy 10:16 and 30:6, which Jewish readers know from the Torah itself. Rashi explains 4:10 as the false prophets' deception of the people, and compares Genesis 3:13.
views.X: Paul takes up the 'circumcision of the heart' (Romans 2:28-29). Some Christian readers compare 4:23-26 with 2 Peter 3:10 and Revelation 6:12-14 as a picture of the end of the world. Some hear Jeremiah's cry in 4:19 as the suffering of a prophet who shares God's pain, and as a figure of Christ's sorrow over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41).
views.F: Some premillennial readers take 4:23-27 as a picture of the end-time judgment on the whole earth, 'a desolation, but not a complete end', followed by restoration. Many readers, Jewish and Christian, take the promise that God will not make a complete end as a pledge that Israel would survive the exile.

deep.b: The four 'I looked' lines run in the order of Genesis 1 reversed or scrambled: the earth and heavens (1:1-2), the lights (1:3, 14-18), the mountains (1:9-10), human beings (1:26-27), birds (1:20-22), and the fruitful land and its cities (Genesis 2:5-9). The phrase tohu wabohu appears only here, in Genesis 1:2 and in Isaiah 34:11. Michael Fishbane argued that the poem is a deliberate undoing of the pattern, as Job 3:3-13 is. Whether Jeremiah knew Genesis 1 in its present form, or both rest on a shared older tradition, is disputed. The Greek says only 'and behold, nothing' (outhen), so the verbal echo is Hebrew only.

Circumcision was the sign of the covenant given to Abraham (Genesis 17). Moses had already said the sign must reach the heart (Deuteronomy 10:16) and that God would one day do it himself (Deuteronomy 30:6). Jeremiah's call in 4:4 joins them, and 9:25-26 says that all nations that practice circumcision, Israel included, are uncircumcised in heart. The New Testament takes up the idea (Romans 2:28-29; Colossians 2:11-12; Acts 7:51) and Christians and Jews have read it differently; for the Christian use see the note on 4:4.

The main differences are given as variants: 4:1-2 (third person for Israel, 'from his mouth', 'reverence', 'praise God in Jerusalem'), 4:11 ('a spirit of error'), 4:19 (pain, and who has heard). Elsewhere the Greek has 'the cities that have walls' in 4:5 and 'flee to Zion' in 4:6. It puts 4:10 as a question and 4:23 as 'nothing'.

echoes: Genesis 1:2; Genesis 12:3; Deuteronomy 10:16; Deuteronomy 30:6; Hosea 10:12; Isaiah 34:11; Job 3:3-13; Zephaniah 1:2-3; Romans 2:28-29; Jeremiah 6:1; Jeremiah 6:22-24; Jeremiah 9:25-26

settings.what: Plow new ground, circumcise your hearts
settings.to: 'The people of Judah and Jerusalem' (4:3), the same hearers as the alarm that follows
settings.when: Not dated. It follows the call to turn back of 3:6-4:2 and comes before the alarm of 4:5.
settings.why: To say what turning back must mean in practice: a new start, with no sowing among thorns, and a change that reaches the heart, before the LORD's anger breaks out like fire.
settings.readers: The exiles, who could read it with Deuteronomy 10:16 and 30:6, the call and the promise that the heart's covering can be removed.

settings.what: The alarm over Judah and Jerusalem
settings.by: The LORD, in a voice that shifts to the prophet's (4:10, 19-22)
settings.to: 'The people of Judah and Jerusalem' (4:5, 11): the people of the land and the city, in the face of an approaching army
settings.when: Not dated. The invader is not named; the poems are set at a time of crisis, whether in the 620s or in Jehoiakim's and Zedekiah's reigns.
settings.why: To make the danger real and the cause plain. The calls to turn (4:1-4, 14), the alarms (4:5-6, 16-17), the vision of undoing (4:23-26) and the cry of the prophet (4:19-22) leave the people in no doubt that the disaster is coming and that it is of their making.
settings.readers: The exiles, who had known the sound of the ram's horn in the siege, and who could read the poems as describing what they had lived through.
views: The poems are set against a nearer northern threat; the best-known form of this view names the Scythians (Herodotus 1.103-106; see the note at 1:14).
The details of the siege (4:16-17) are matched with Nebuchadnezzar's campaigns of 597-586.

title: Is there one honest person?
sum: The LORD sends Jeremiah through the streets and squares of Jerusalem to find one person who acts with justice and looks for faithfulness. If he finds one, the LORD will forgive the city (5:1). The search fails: they swear 'As the LORD lives' but swear to a lie (5:2), and neither blows nor discipline moves them (5:3). Jeremiah first thinks that the poor are foolish because they do not know the LORD's way, and then finds the great ones have broken the yoke too (5:4-5). A lion, a wolf and a leopard are their punishment (5:6).

The charges are adultery and denying the LORD: they say 'He will do nothing' (5:7-13). The LORD answers that his words in Jeremiah's mouth will be fire, and that a nation from far away with a language they do not know will eat their harvest, children, flocks, vines and cities (5:14-17). Even then he will not make a complete end, and when they ask why, the answer is that they served foreign gods in their land and will serve outsiders in another (5:18-19). The people have eyes and cannot see, and they fear no one, though the sea itself keeps to its limit (5:20-24). The city's rich grow fat by fraud and ignore the orphan and the poor (5:25-29). The chapter ends with the horror that prophets lie, priests rule at their side, and the people love it (5:30-31).
readings: Read as the LORD's search
The chapter is a test of the city: the LORD offers to forgive, and the failure to find one person justifies the sentence.
Read as a portrait of society

Others stress the sketches of the rich who prosper by fraud, the leaders who deny the LORD, and the prophets and priests who flatter: a portrait of Judah's social and religious failure in the last decades.

views.H: The chapter is undated. The sins described, fraud among the rich, denial of judgment, oppression of orphans and false prophecy, fit the last decades before 586. Foreign tongue (5:15) and the destruction of the fortified cities (5:17) fit Babylon's armies, although they are not named.
views.C: Scholars often treat 5:1-17 as a unit of poetry, with 5:18-19 as a prose addition from the exile since it answers the exiles' question 'Why?' in the language of Deuteronomy 29. The Greek lacks two phrases and a line in 5:15-16 (see the variants) and adds olive trees in 5:17.
views.X: Christian preachers use 5:1 with Romans 3:10-12 to say that no one is righteous, and see in the search for one just person a pointer to Christ. 5:21 ('eyes that do not see') is echoed in Mark 8:18 (compare Isaiah 6:9-10 and Ezekiel 12:2).
views.F: 5:18 ('I will not make a complete end') is taken by many, Jewish and Christian, as the promise that Israel will not be destroyed.

deep.b: The Greek leaves out 'an enduring nation, an ancient nation' (5:15) and 'Their quiver is like an open grave' (5:16), and adds 'your olive trees' in 5:17. In 5:7 it reads 'they lodged', in 5:31 'they clapped their hands', and in 5:14 it gives 'the Lord Almighty' for 'the LORD, the God of Armies'. These differences may reflect an earlier form of the Hebrew; none can be checked against a scroll of Jeremiah, since none preserves chapter 5.

The words 'It is not he' are the people's answer to the prophets' warning. They do not argue that the LORD does not exist; they say that he does not act. This is the same logic as the 'Peace, peace' of 6:14: if no disaster is coming, no repentance is needed. Zephaniah 1:12 has the same attitude in the people who say, 'The LORD will not do good, and he will not do harm.'

echoes: Genesis 18:22-33; Ezekiel 22:30; Deuteronomy 28:49-52; Deuteronomy 29:24-28; Job 38:8-11; Psalm 104:9; Hosea 13:7-8; Jeremiah 1:9; Jeremiah 23:29; Romans 3:10-12

settings.what: The search of Jerusalem and the verdict
settings.to: Jerusalem's people, rich and poor; the 'great ones'; priests and prophets
settings.when: Not dated. Perhaps Jehoiakim's reign (609-598), when social wrongs and false confidence both ran high; others place the poems earlier or later.
settings.why: To show that the city has no ground to stand on. Jeremiah first guesses that the poor, who have had little teaching, may be excused, and then finds that the great, who know the LORD's way, have broken the yoke too (5:4-5). The message answers the false confidence of 5:12.
settings.readers: The exiles, reading the summary of why Jerusalem could not be spared (5:19).
views: The social wrongs and the false confidence fit the years after 609, when Jerusalem trusted its Temple (compare 7:1-15).
The foreign nation of 5:15 is not named, so the poems may be early warnings; the chapter itself gives no date.

title: Disaster looks down from the north
sum: The people of Benjamin are told to flee south, out of Jerusalem: the ram's horn is blown at Tekoa and a signal raised at Beth-hakkerem, because disaster peers down from the north (6:1). Daughter Zion is compared to a dainty pasture, and shepherds will come to her with their flocks and tents (6:2-3); the other reading of 6:2 is 'I will destroy her'. The attackers speak: they will 'consecrate war' and attack at noon or by night (6:4-5). The LORD commands them to cut down trees and pile up an assault ramp against Jerusalem, since it is a city of oppression, where evil stays fresh like water in a well (6:6-8).

The prophet asks who will listen; their ears are uncircumcised, and he is full of the LORD's fury (6:9-11). From the least to the greatest all are greedy, and prophet and priest deal in lies, treating a broken nation as scratched: 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace (6:12-15). The LORD offers a way: stand at the crossroads and ask for the ancient paths, and walk the good road; but they answer, 'We will not walk on it' (6:16-17). The nations are called as witnesses, and the offerings are not accepted (6:18-21). A new army, cruel and from the far north, arrives (6:22-26). The chapter ends with Jeremiah as a tester of metals, and the verdict that the people are 'rejected silver' because the refining has failed (6:27-30).
readings: Read as the climax of the first section
Chapters 4-6 build to this: the alarm of 4:5-6 is repeated in 6:1; the cry for Zion in 4:31 returns in 6:23-26; the decision is final in 6:30.
Read as a set of separate poems
Others see 6:1-8, 9-15, 16-21, 22-26 and 27-30 as five poems that were grouped by theme, and 6:13-15 as a unit that is repeated in 8:10-12.

views.H: The ram's horn at Tekoa, the signal at Beth-hakkerem and the siege ramp suggest a time when Babylon's army was near, and many date the chapter to the reign of Jehoiakim or Zedekiah. Others keep it in the early years.
views.C: Scholars notice the repeated lines (6:13-15 and 8:10-12; 6:22-24 and 50:41-43) and ask which is original. The Greek of 6:2, 6:11 and 6:18 differs from the Hebrew (see the notes). The Greek calls the prophet of 6:13 a 'false prophet' (pseudoprophetes), a word it uses in many places where the Hebrew has only 'prophet'.
views.J: Rashi's only comment on 6:16 names the Hebrew word for 'rest', marge'a.
views.X: Jesus' words 'you will find rest for your souls' (Matthew 11:29) use the wording of 6:16 in the Hebrew, and some Christian readers take the 'good way' to be Christ himself. 6:14 is echoed in 1 Thessalonians 5:3. 6:10 'uncircumcised ears' is used by Stephen (Acts 7:51). 6:20 is read with Isaiah 1:11-17 as God's refusal of worship without justice.
views.F: Most readers take the chapter as fulfilled in 586. Some Christian readers connect the army from the far north with the northern invader of Ezekiel 38-39, but Jeremiah does not make that link.

deep.b: The charge against the prophets and priests in 6:13-15 is about what they said and how they said it. They treated the 'crash' of the nation as a scratch and called out 'Peace'. The same lines in 8:11 are followed by Jeremiah's own lament, and the confrontation with Hananiah in chapter 28 shows how the two kinds of prophecy met in the open. The Law's test of a prophet (Deuteronomy 18:21-22) is cited there; Jeremiah's own test is that the prophets 'have not stood in the council of the LORD' (23:18, 22).

The Greek differs in 6:2 ('your height will be taken away'), 6:6 ('pour out force on Jerusalem'), 6:7 ('as a cistern keeps cool its water'), 6:11 (God says 'I have filled my anger and held back'), 6:13 ('from priest to false prophet'), 6:16 ('purification'), 6:18 ('shepherds'), 6:27 ('a tester among tested peoples') and 6:29 (the bellows and the lead give out). No scroll of Jeremiah preserves any readable word of chapter 6, so the Greek is the only early witness to compare; some of its differences come from the translator.

echoes: Deuteronomy 20:19-20; Deuteronomy 28:49; Isaiah 1:11-17; Isaiah 1:22-25; Ezekiel 13:10; Ezekiel 22:17-22; Micah 3:5; Matthew 11:28-30; Acts 7:51; 1 Thessalonians 5:3; Jeremiah 8:10-12; Jeremiah 50:41-43

settings.what: The siege poems and the verdict on the refining
settings.by: The LORD, and the prophet in 6:10-11, 27
settings.to: The people of Benjamin and Jerusalem (6:1); the nations as witnesses (6:18-19); the prophet himself (6:27)
settings.when: Not dated. The images of siege fit the time of Babylon's campaigns, or Jeremiah's early picture of a northern foe.
settings.why: To tell the people that the city is about to be besieged and that no worship or prophetic reassurance will save it. The offer of the ancient paths (6:16) is the last open door. The closing image makes Jeremiah a tester of metals to show that the people have been tested and found to be dross.
settings.readers: The exiles, who would read 6:16-17 as the hearing that was refused and 6:27-30 as the book's summary of the pre-exilic generation.
views: The siege poems are Jeremiah's first view of a northern invader, whose identity he left open.
Spoken in Jehoiakim's or Zedekiah's time
At least the siege-ramp verses are dated to the Babylonian war.
